channel_b.verbatim: Bank of England, Financial Stability Report July 2026 (7 July 2026): "The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has found that the latest frontier models (eg Anthropic's Mythos Preview and OpenAI's GPT 5.5) represent a clear step up from earlier models in an area where cyber performance was already improving quickly (Chart 3.1). ... Recent frontier models have also successfully completed both of AISI's harder 'cyber range' tests - simulated attacks against small, undefended company networks requiring sustained planning and execution. This is a notable result because ... no previous model had completed either range." | GDS/DSIT guidance, 14 May 2026: "The UK AI Security Institute reports that recent frontier models show materially-stronger cyber capability in controlled evaluations. Some examples of this are ... the AISI Work Blog, Our evaluation of Claude Mythos Preview's cyber capabilities, 13 April 2026." | DSIT/Cabinet Office open letter, 15 April 2026: "Recent tests of advanced AI models, including the AISI's evaluation of Anthropic's Mythos, indicate that AI cyber capabilities are accelerating even faster than had been previously envisaged."
channel_b.policy_response: Sustained, multi-channel UK engagement with this evaluation, all of it non-binding. (a) DSIT/Cabinet Office open letter to business leaders (15 April 2026) citing the AISI Mythos evaluation and launching a voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge; (b) Security Minister's CYBERUK speech (22 April) and the Secretary of State's RUSI speech (28 April), both stating AISI tested and verified the Mythos claims; (c) DSIT news release (11 May) citing AISI research on Mythos; (d) cross-government GDS/DSIT guidance (14 May) citing the report by name as a reason to tighten the open-code-by-default posture; (e) DSIT/NCSC operational case study (12 June); (f) Bank of England Financial Policy Committee Financial Stability Report (7 July) treating AISI's Mythos and GPT-5.5 results as an input to the UK systemic cyber-risk assessment; (g) repeated ministerial statements in the Lords, including confirmation that government 'gave advice to our companies' in light of the risks Mythos posed. No law, regulation or regulatory order imposes a mandatory requirement arising from this finding; the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill before Parliament is not tied to it.

Nothing found is enforceable: an open letter, speeches, advisory guidance, a case study, an FPC risk assessment and parliamentary debate all fall short of a mandatory requirement, and a government request complied with voluntarily is expressly not binding.
